title.en: Adopt a published notation and follow it exactly

summary: When a subject has an established notation, use it exactly, including the orientation convention that defines a positive turn.
objective: Make a scene interoperable with the vocabulary its users already have.
applies_when: Moves, states or structures are named in text alongside the visual.
Users may type sequences, paste scrambles or compare with external material.
A tutorial, solution or algorithm is displayed.
example_prompts: Accept standard cube notation and animate the moves.
Show the move names as I turn the faces.
negative_signals: Invented puzzles with no established notation, which need their own defined vocabulary.
Purely visual interaction with no textual move vocabulary.
not_for: Invented puzzles with no established notation, which need their own defined vocabulary.
Purely visual interaction with no textual move vocabulary.

principles: A published notation is a shared interface. Regulation notation for cube face moves names the front, back, right, left, upper and bottom faces, treats the plain letter as a ninety degree clockwise turn seen from that face, marks the counter-clockwise turn with a prime and the half turn with a two.

The orientation convention is the part most often lost: clockwise as seen from the moving face is not the same as clockwise from a fixed camera, and a mirrored implementation is consistent with itself while disagreeing with every published algorithm.
Interoperability is the payoff: a scene that reads standard notation can accept community scrambles and solutions without translation.
Where a scene extends beyond the standard vocabulary, the extension should be marked as an extension rather than blended in silently.
implementation: Implement the notation from the published definition rather than from memory, and record which document and version was used.
Verify the turn direction against the convention with a labelled test, since a sign error is invisible on a symmetric puzzle.
Support both reading and writing the notation, so a sequence performed by hand can be exported as text.
Show the move name as each move is performed, which turns the interface into a way to learn the notation.
Mark any non-standard moves or extensions distinctly in both directions of translation.
observable_checks: Apply a well-known published sequence and confirm the resulting pattern matches the published outcome.
Perform a move and its prime and confirm the state returns and the notation output matches.
Paste a scramble, then export it, and confirm the text round-trips.
Check a single face turn against the convention with the camera behind the puzzle, where mirroring errors become obvious.

creative_affordances: A friendlier alternative notation can be offered alongside the standard one as long as the standard is supported.
Invented puzzles deserve a clearly defined notation of their own, designed with the same care.
known_limits: Authored convention guidance citing face-turn notation from a published regulation; wide moves, slice moves and rotations were not read in this session.
Notation for other puzzle types differs and needs its own source.

claims.statement: In the World Cube Association notation for cube puzzles the letters F, B, R, L, U and D denote ninety degree clockwise turns of the front, back, right, left, upper and bottom faces, a prime denotes the counter-clockwise ninety degree turn and a following two denotes a one hundred and eighty degree turn.
claims.scope: Face-move notation for cube puzzles; wide moves, slice moves and whole-puzzle rotations are not covered by this claim.
